articles.body: The Krestianstvo Abstract Holographic Computer (AHC) medium can now hold the quantum condensate dynamics in the field. Bose–Einstein condensates (BECs) are native c-fields. Fermionic superfluids use Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) pairing on the medium’s own dispersion and matrix-free. Run live Core Principles: Field Medium Over Matrices Traditional quantum simulations rely on large Hamiltonian matrices, Fock-space occupation numbers, and single-particle orbital expansions. In contrast, the Krestianstvo Abstract Holographic Computer medium treats a condensate as a macroscopic continuum wavefunction living on a closed periodic grid (torus). Each slot owns a contiguous complex field representing a coherent quantum state or condensate reservoir.

articles.title: Chrome Extension Service Worker: 4 Rules to Survive Shutdown
articles.excerpt: Originally published on ExtensionLaunch. Your Chrome extension service worker works perfectly while you test it, then silently drops state, misses events or "forgets" a timer once real users have it.…
articles.body: Originally published on ExtensionLaunch . Your Chrome extension service worker works perfectly while you test it, then silently drops state, misses events or "forgets" a timer once real users have it. That is not a Chrome bug: in Manifest V3 the background script is built to stop and restart, and your code has to expect it. Here are the shutdown rules and four habits that keep an extension working through them. "Service worker (inactive)" is not an error On chrome://extensions you will often see service worker (inactive) next to your extension. It only means the worker is stopped right now. Chrome starts the worker when something it listens for happens (a toolbar click, a message, an alarm) and stops it again when things go quiet.

articles.title: Modeling Late TikTok Shop Refunds Without Rewriting Yesterday's Profit
articles.excerpt: A daily profit report is easy to build when every order, refund, and fee arrives on the day it occurred. Real marketplace operations are messier: refunds arrive late, commission estimates are finalize…
articles.body: A daily profit report is easy to build when every order, refund, and fee arrives on the day it occurred. Real marketplace operations are messier: refunds arrive late, commission estimates are finalized later, and settlement corrections can appear days after the sale. If the reporting layer overwrites yesterday's numbers whenever new information arrives, operators lose two things at once: a stable history and the ability to learn from the correction. Separate event time from posting time Store two timestamps for every money movement: event date — when the sale, refund, or fee is considered to have happened; posting date — when the platform reported the adjustment to your system. This lets you show a stable event-date view while also surfacing when new corrections were discovered.

articles.title: How to copy screenshots and errors to coding agents
articles.excerpt: Ctrl+V pastes a screenshot into Claude Code. But by the time I ask for a fix I've copied three things from three apps. A prompt hook hands the agent all of them, so the prompt is just "fix this error"…
articles.body: Ctrl+V pastes a screenshot into Claude Code. But by the time I ask for a fix I've copied three things from three apps. A prompt hook hands the agent all of them, so the prompt is just "fix this error". Key findings Over five weeks, a prompt hook gave my coding agents what I had just copied with 274 prompts. Under its current three-clip cap, more than one in four of those prompts carried several clips, and 18% mixed apps: a screenshot, a console line, a terminal command. Screenshots go to the agent as their text plus the image's file path. When the path was there, the agent opened the image only 6 times out of 70. The text was enough, at no more than about 150 tokens instead of roughly 1,500 for the image.

articles.title: This supernova impostor baffled astronomers for 15 years — until they found a hidden black hole feeding on an unstable star
articles.excerpt: A hidden black hole or neutron star companion to an unstable massive star is causing the system to erupt in light that mimics a supernova explosion.
articles.body: A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered. When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.

articles.body: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P . To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement. The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired. When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space . The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down. Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it . Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.
